reason: The text consistently portrays the Hebrews as a distinct people and nation with collective identity and organizational structure, beyond merely familial or religious identity. Key evidence includes: (1) Repeated references to 'עַם' (people/nation) and 'בְנֵי־ יִשְׂרָאֵל' (children of Israel) as a collective entity; (2) Description of their multiplication and growth as a people occupying land; (3) Their organization under leaders, judges, and elders in hierarchical structures; (4) Collective laws and commandments given to them as a people; (5) Encampment and movement as unified national forces ('צִבְאֹתָם' - their hosts/armies); (6) Establishment of the 'עֲדַת בְּנֵי־ יִשְׂרָאֵל' (congregation of Israel) as a formal collective body. While genealogy and religious devotion are also present, the text emphasizes their identity as an organized nation with legal systems, territorial claims, and national structure that transcends mere family kinship or religious adherence.
